passage: At two in the morning in Singapore, Chen typed a long post about how much she hated school, how her parents were being unfair and how she felt like nobody understood her. She added the name of her school and a photo of her uniform. Her thumb hovered over 'Post'. She messaged her friend Oskar: 'Should I put this up?' He replied at once, 'Wait until morning. And take out the school name, strangers can see that.' Chen put the phone face-down. In the morning she deleted the school name and the photo and read the post again. It felt too raw now. She sent it privately to Oskar instead, and they talked at recess about what was actually bothering her.

qa.q: What did Chen add to the post besides her feelings?
qa.a: She added the name of her school and a photo of her uniform.

qa.q: Why was Chen tempted to post at two in the morning?
qa.a: She felt misunderstood and wanted someone to hear how she felt, and the late hour made her feelings seem larger. She may also have wanted attention or support.

qa.q: What worked about Oskar's advice?
qa.a: He told her to wait until morning, take out identifying details and then talk to him, which let her pause and choose a trusted audience.

qa.q: How might her parents have felt if they had seen the post?
qa.a: They may have felt hurt and worried, and it could have made the conversation harder.

grounding: A teen pauses before posting personal details and feelings, and turns to a trusted friend instead.

passage: Mr Francis wrote on the whiteboard: 'What would you never post?' and gave the class of Year Ten two minutes. Samir, who had posted his home address and a photo of his door key ring the week before to show off a new lock, went quiet. Someone said, 'Your address.' Someone else said, 'When you're really upset.' Francis asked the class, 'If it stays online for years, who might see it?' Samir put his hand up slowly. "Someone could read my old posts when I apply for a course." After class he stayed. "I want to delete the address one. Can you help?" Francis nodded. "Let's do it now. And who would you talk to for the big stuff?" Samir thought. "My cousin."

qa.q: What did Mr Francis write on the whiteboard?
qa.a: He wrote: 'What would you never post?'

qa.q: What was Samir probably feeling when he went quiet?
qa.a: He was probably embarrassed and worried, because he had posted his address and key ring photo, and the discussion made him see the risk. Asking to delete it shows he wanted to fix it.

qa.q: What small step helped Samir?
qa.a: He asked his teacher to help him delete the post right away and named his cousin as someone to talk to about heavy topics.

qa.q: How might Mr Francis have felt when Samir stayed after class?
qa.a: He may have felt pleased that the lesson reached Samir and that Samir trusted him with the problem.

grounding: A teen learns to consider permanence and audience, and uses trusted people for heavy topics, in a class.

passage:
Simran didi,
You said to write if I ever wanted to post something big. So I'm writing instead of posting.
Last night Mumma and Papa had the loudest fight I've ever heard. I sat on my bed and typed a long story for my public page. Everything. What they shouted, how I felt, even that I think they might split up. My finger was on the button.
Then I remembered what you said: "The internet doesn't forget, and your classmates' parents read it too." I thought about Papa's colleagues seeing it. About me seeing it in five years.
So I deleted it. But I still feel all of it. I just don't want 300 people to hold it. I want you to.
Can we talk on Sunday? I'll call after lunch.
Pranav

qa.q: When does Pranav plan to call Simran?
qa.a: Pranav will call after lunch on Sunday.

qa.q: What was Pranav feeling while typing the post?
qa.a: Pranav felt upset and scared after the fight, needing to let it all out and get some support.

qa.q: What small step helped Pranav protect the family's privacy?
qa.a: Pausing to remember Simran's advice about permanence and audience, deleting the post, and writing to a trusted cousin instead.

qa.q: How might Pranav's parents have felt if the post had gone up?
qa.a: They would probably have felt exposed and hurt that a private fight was read by classmates' parents and colleagues.

grounding: The letter shows a teenager pausing before an overshare, weighing permanence and audience, and turning to a trusted person for a heavy topic.

passage:
Asif, you asked for my worst posting mistake. Okay. I'm Uday, and last year I posted a birthday photo that showed everything. My school badge, the name of my building, even the gate number behind me. Plus a caption about how nobody at home remembered my birthday, so I was alone all evening.
I wanted someone to notice. People did. Lots of hearts. But also a stranger commented, "Sad bro, I live near your building, want to hang out?"
That's when my stomach dropped.
I showed my dad, and he helped me delete it and report the comment. He also said something I didn't expect: "I'm sorry we forgot. Next time, tell me, not the internet."
Now I pause before posting. I ask, who'll see this, and will I be okay with it next year? The heavy stuff I tell my friend Asma, who actually texts back.

qa.q: What did Uday's photo show behind him?
qa.a: It showed Uday's school badge, the name of the building, and even the gate number.

qa.q: What was Uday feeling when he posted the caption?
qa.a: Uday felt lonely and hurt that nobody at home remembered the birthday, and wanted someone to notice.

qa.q: What does Uday do now before posting?
qa.a: Uday pauses and asks who will see it and whether he'll be okay with it next year, and takes heavy things to his friend Asma.

qa.q: How might Uday's dad have felt reading the post?
qa.a: He probably felt guilty and worried, sorry they had forgotten the birthday and alarmed by the stranger's comment.

grounding: The spoken account shows a teenager oversharing personal details and feelings publicly for attention, and learning to pause and use trusted friends.

passage:
I'm Amandeep, and I sit next to Joseph in chemistry. On Monday I saw him typing on his phone under the desk for the whole period. At break he showed me: a long public post about his grandfather being in hospital, the ward number, what the doctor said, and a line about crying every night.
I didn't know what he wanted from it. Maybe support. Maybe just to say it somewhere.
I said, "It's really sad. Do you want everyone at school to know the ward number and all that?"
He looked at it again. He was quiet for a bit.
"No. I just wanted someone to know."
"I know now," I said.
He deleted the post and sent one line instead: "Family's going through a tough time, please keep us in your thoughts." Then he told me the rest at lunch, and I walked him to the bus.

qa.q: What details did Joseph's post include?
qa.a: It included his grandfather being in hospital, the ward number, what the doctor said, and a line about crying every night.

qa.q: What was Joseph feeling when he wrote the long post?
qa.a: Joseph was sad and worried about his grandfather, and seemed to want someone to know and care.

qa.q: Which of Amandeep's choices helped, and why?
qa.a: Asking gently about the ward number and audience, then offering to listen, helped Joseph keep private details safe and still get support.

qa.q: How might Joseph's grandfather feel if his ward number and illness were posted publicly?
qa.a: He might feel his privacy was exposed at a vulnerable time, which is one reason pausing before posting matters.

grounding: A classmate's account shows a teenager oversharing personal details while seeking support and choosing a trusted friend for the heavy part.

passage:
Tuesday, 1 a.m. After another loud night at home, Sonali typed a long public story: "my parents screamed for 2 hours again, I hate this house, I can't breathe here." She added the name of her street and a photo from her window, and posted it.
Wednesday. By first period, forty people had seen it. Two classmates sent crying faces; an account she didn't know wrote, "dm me, I'll listen 😘". Her stomach dropped. Varun found her near the water cooler. "Hey. I saw your story. You okay? Maybe take the street name down, anyone can see that." She deleted it right there. At lunch they talked on the steps, and he told her the school counsellor had helped him when his parents split up.
The next Monday. Another bad night. Sonali opened the app, typed three lines, stopped, and read them as if she were a stranger. Then she deleted the draft and texted Varun instead. In the morning she knocked on the counsellor's door.

qa.q: How many people had seen the story by first period?
qa.a: Forty people had seen it by first period.

qa.q: What was Sonali feeling when the unknown account wrote to her?
qa.a: Sonali felt exposed and alarmed, her stomach dropping, as she realised strangers could see her street and feelings; she may also have felt some shame at how public it was.

qa.q: What small step helped Sonali the next Monday?
qa.a: Sonali read the draft as a stranger would, deleted it, texted Varun instead and went to the counsellor in the morning, keeping heavy things with trusted people.

qa.q: How might Varun have felt reading the 1 a.m. story?
qa.a: Varun was probably worried about both Sonali's feelings and her safety, which is why he asked if she was okay and pointed out the street name.

grounding: It shows a teenager posting personal details and feelings publicly in distress, then learning to pause, think about audience and permanence, and turn to trusted people instead.
